common_name: Fama Daylily (Rounded Rose-Pink Daylily with Gold Edge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Fama is a cold-hardy Midwestern daylily bred for substance and form, producing broad, rounded, rose-pink flowers edged in a narrow band of gold.

directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, spacing clumps 15 to 20 inches apart to allow for several seasons of increase. Fama produces heavily substanced, rounded rose-pink flowers with a ruffled gold edge and a lightly textured surface that give the bloom a full, formal appearance against the strap-shaped foliage. Bred for reliable performance in cold-winter climates, it bulks up into a vigorous, floriferous clump within two to three years and holds its flower form well through heat and humidity. Water regularly during the bloom period and divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to sustain bloom count and flower quality.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Hemerocallis Cultivars

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Ruffled Masterpiece bears round, heavily ruffled cream-to-gold flowers with substantial petals that hold up well through heat.

directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Ruffled Masterpiece produces large, rounded, cream-to-pale-gold flowers with heavily ruffled, gold-dusted petal edges and good substance, giving each bloom a full, polished look that holds up through midday sun and summer heat. The clump builds steadily into a dense, floriferous stand of strap-shaped foliage topped by well-branched scapes carrying numerous buds for an extended bloom season. It performs reliably in cold-winter regions and is undemanding once established, needing only routine watering and occasional feeding. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain bloom size and count.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Hemerocallis Cultivars

common_name: Smuggler's Gold Daylily (Classic Gold Self Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Smuggler's Gold is an older, widely grown daylily cultivar with clear golden-yellow flowers of good substance on well-branched scapes.

directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Smuggler's Gold carries clear, unpatterned golden-yellow flowers of good substance and classic daylily form on sturdy, well-branched scapes that rise above the arching, strap-shaped foliage. It is a vigorous, easy-care increaser that has remained in circulation for decades thanks to its dependable midsummer bloom and tolerance of a wide range of soils and climates. The plain gold coloring combines readily with patterned and eyed daylily cultivars in mixed borders. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to keep bloom production strong.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Hemerocallis Cultivars

planting.note: Plant hollow stem-cane cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in moist, fertile soil after the last frost; this larger relative of Dahlia imperialis forms thick, woody, bamboo-like canes that can exceed those of the common tree dahlia in girth and height over a single growing season.

directions: Plant cane cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, away from wind that could snap the tall, hollow stems. Giant tree dahlia is one of the largest species in the tree dahlia group, pushing up thick, jointed, bamboo-like canes well over ten feet tall in a single season before topping out with clusters of large single flowers in the final weeks of autumn. Like its better-known relative Dahlia imperialis, it is strongly day-length sensitive and will not begin flowering until the shortening days of late fall, so gardeners outside the mildest climates may see foliage and cane growth but few or no open flowers before frost ends the season. In zone 9 and warmer it persists as a woody-based perennial, resprouting from the base each spring. Protect the root zone with heavy mulch where winter cold threatens the crown.

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in moist, fertile soil after the last frost; this tree dahlia relative has noticeably more slender, lighter canes than Dahlia imperialis, making it easier to stake and manage in garden settings.

directions: Plant stem cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. The slender-stemmed tree dahlia shares the fall-blooming, day-length-sensitive habit of its larger relatives but grows on noticeably thinner, more pliable canes, making it a more manageable choice for gardeners who want the architectural tree-dahlia look without the massive, hard-to-stake stems of the giant species. Flowers open in pink to lavender shades along the upper canes once autumn days shorten, typically later in the season than hybrid garden dahlias. In frost-free or near-frost-free gardens it persists from year to year as a woody-based perennial; elsewhere it can be grown as a dramatic annual or overwintered indoors as rooted cane sections. Mulch the base heavily before winter in borderline zones.
sources: International Dahlia Register and Classified List

planting.note: Plant hollow cane cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in moist, fertile soil after the last frost; the bell tree dahlia is distinguished from other tree dahlias by its nodding, bell-shaped flowers rather than flat, open faces.

directions: Plant cane cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Bell tree dahlia grows on tall, hollow, bamboo-like canes in the manner of its tree dahlia relatives, but its flowers hang in distinctive nodding bells rather than opening flat, giving the autumn display a softer, more pendulous look. Like other species in this group it is strongly day-length sensitive, beginning to flower only as autumn days shorten, so plants in marginal climates may need to be grown in containers and brought under cover to complete their bloom cycle before frost. Where winters stay mild it becomes a permanent, woody-based perennial that regrows taller each year. Provide a sheltered spot out of strong wind, since the tall canes can be brittle at the joints.
sources: International Dahlia Register and Classified List

planting.note: Plant hollow stem-cane cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in moist, fertile soil after the last frost; this white-flowered form of the tree dahlia matches the species' giant bamboo-like habit but opens pure white single flowers instead of the typical lavender-pink.

directions: Plant stem cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. This white-flowered selection of the tree dahlia reaches the same towering, 10-to-20-foot stature as the species on stout, hollow, cane-like stems, but opens clean white single flowers with yellow centers instead of the usual lavender-pink, giving a brighter, more luminous display against the dark green foliage. Flowering is strictly day-length triggered and begins only as autumn days shorten, so the show arrives in the final weeks before frost in most gardens. In zone 9 and frost-free climates it persists as a permanent, woody-based perennial that regrows from the prior season's canes; in zone 8 it is better treated as a die-back perennial grown from stored tuberous roots. Harvest cane sections before hard frost to propagate new plants the following spring.
sources: International Dahlia Register and Classified List
